news.title: Jensen Huang admits affair with suspected Chinese spy as Nvidia's board opens a probe
news.summary: In a Sunday memo to staff, Nvidia's CEO admitted a relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US intelligence believes was recruited by China, and said he takes full responsibility. Nvidia's board has hired outside counsel for an independent review and says it has seen no sign that company secrets were compromised.

news.title: Trump says he doesn't mind AI guardrails as long as the US stays ahead of China
news.summary: In a 60 Minutes interview, the president said AI's risks can be managed and pointed to the Justice Department as the body that would manage them. He did not say which specific rules he would be willing to sign.

news.title: Anthropic reportedly buys $3.4 billion of gas generators to power its data centers
news.summary: Citing the Financial Times, CNBC reports that Anthropic took over about 1.7 gigawatts of Caterpillar gas generators originally ordered by OnePWR. The deal shows AI labs moving to secure their own power rather than wait for grid connections.

news.title: Staff at the US AI safety testing center are now informally reporting to the White House
news.summary: The Commerce Department's AI testing center, CAISSI, has no permanent head, has stopped publishing its research, and its officials were asked to report informally to a White House office. Critics worry this could soften its findings; its budget is about $10 million a year, roughly an eighth of the UK equivalent.

news.title: Megaspeed executive was recruited to spy on Nvidia's CEO, US intelligence memo says
news.summary: A classified memo drafted under Secretary of State Rubio concluded that the executive at the centre of the Huang story was working for China's Ministry of State Security. China's foreign ministry has called the claims unsubstantiated.

news.title: DeepSeek's open-source agent app Harness passes 1.5 million daily users
news.summary: DeepSeek disclosed usage numbers for Harness for the first time: 1.54 million daily active users, up more than a million in a month. The platform is processing about 92 trillion tokens a day.

news.title: Nvidia, Rebellions and SK Telecom agree to link Korean AI chips with Nvidia GPUs
news.summary: At Nvidia AI Day Seoul, the three companies signed a memorandum to connect Rebellions' inference chips to Nvidia GPUs through NVLink Fusion inside SK Telecom data centers. Deployment of Rebellions' R200 chip is targeted for 2028.

news.title: Shanghai AI Lab study: an AI agent improved a model by hand-editing 1,023 weights
news.summary: Using GPT-6 Astra as the editor, researchers lifted a small Qwen model's MATH-500 score by 29 points without any training. The gains were uneven, though, and several edits failed to hold on unseen test questions (see today's LLM paper).

news.title: Nearly one in five US workers replaced by AI were later asked back
news.summary: A survey by assessment firm SHL found 19.1% of US workers laid off or replaced by AI were later invited to return by the same employer. Many asked for higher pay or written job-security promises before agreeing.

papers.title: Training-Independent Validation of a Learning-Based Controller for Stunt Maneuvers
papers.tldr: Testing a learned driving controller only the way it was trained makes it look safer than it is, so the authors test it under changed physics and independent safety rules, using simulation to pick which real-car trials are safe.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
This paper shows that a self-driving controller can look great when tested the way it was trained, and proposes a tougher, separate way to test it before putting it on a real car.

## Background you need
Many vehicle controllers today are learned: an AI policy is trained, usually in simulation, to steer, brake and accelerate. Validation is the step where engineers check that the controller is safe enough to deploy. Stunt maneuvers here mean extreme moves at the edge of grip, such as hard drifts or sharp heading changes. Sideslip is how much a car slides sideways relative to where it is pointing, and yaw rate is how fast it is turning.

## The problem
Learned controllers are often validated under the same conditions and scoring rules used to train them. That is like a student grading their own exam with the answer key they studied. The controller looks reliable, but only because the test matches its practice.

On real roads, things change: tire grip, vehicle weight, road surface. And the score used in training may not capture what "safe" really means. For stunt-level moves, a bad test can lead to a crash. Testing these moves on a real car is risky, so engineers need a way to choose which real trials are safe to try.

## The idea
Think of a driving school. A good examiner does not just repeat the practice route. They change the weather, pick a different car, and judge by safety rules the student was never told about. That is "training-independent" validation.

The authors apply this idea to a learned stunt controller. They vary physical settings that were frozen during training. They also judge results with acceptance rules that were not part of the training goal.

## How it works
1. **Pick a controller to test.** They use G-Maneuver, a learned policy reported to succeed 90.11% of the time on its own terms.
2. **Change the hidden assumptions.** They vary physical parameters that training held fixed, to see how the controller copes with conditions it never saw.
3. **Use outside safety rules.** They apply acceptance criteria not used in training, guided by automotive safety analysis frameworks and coverage tests (checks that the tests span the important conditions).
4. **Loop between simulation and reality.** In a Sim2Real2Sim loop, simulation first marks "safe zones" where a real trial is unlikely to go wrong. Real-car trials run only there. Real results then feed back to check the simulator.
5. **Compare indicators.** They check which measurements agree between simulation and the real car, to know which ones can be trusted for future decisions.

## Results
The choice of score turned out to matter a lot. A looser score based only on the final heading of the car ranked the worst setting as the best. In other words, a sloppy metric could have approved the most dangerous configuration.

Only 16.9% of candidate settings passed the safety screen for real-vehicle trials. That shows how much of the space that looks fine in training is not safe to try for real.

Three indicators matched well between simulation and the real car: heading change, sideslip, and yaw rate scaled by speed. Indicators based on tire forces and body roll did not match. The authors conclude the first group can be trusted to support safe deployment decisions.

## Why it matters
As more vehicle control is learned rather than hand-designed, testing becomes the main safety barrier. This work gives engineers a concrete warning and a recipe. The warning: a controller's headline success rate can hide serious weaknesses. The recipe: test outside training conditions, use independent safety rules, and trust only the measurements that hold up in reality.

## Caveats
This summary is based on the paper's abstract; we could not access the full text, so details on the vehicle and test counts are limited. The study covers one controller and one class of stunt maneuvers. Force and roll indicators did not transfer, so some important safety signals remain hard to check in simulation. Whether the approach scales to everyday driving is untested here.

## Key terms
- **Learned controller:** an AI policy trained to drive, rather than hand-written rules.
- **Validation:** checking a controller is safe before it is deployed.
- **Sideslip:** how much a car slides sideways relative to its heading.
- **Yaw rate:** how quickly the car is rotating left or right.
- **Sim2Real2Sim:** using simulation to choose safe real tests, then using real results to check the simulation.
- **Acceptance criteria:** the rules a test result must meet to count as a pass.

papers.title: FastAFD: When Does Attention-FFN Disaggregation Pay on Rack-Scale NVLink?
papers.tldr: Putting a Mixture-of-Experts model's attention and expert layers on separate GPUs lets each GPU serve more users, giving about 1.4x more tokens per GPU on Nvidia GB200 NVL72 racks.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
FastAFD splits a large AI model across two kinds of GPU workers, one for "reading the conversation" and one for "thinking with experts," and gets about 1.4 times more output per GPU on Nvidia's newest rack-scale systems.

## Background you need
Many big language models today are Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. Instead of one giant network, they have many smaller "expert" sub-networks, and each word is sent to only a few of them. Each layer of the model has two parts: attention (looking back over the conversation so far) and the expert layer (doing the heavy computation). Attention depends on the KV cache, which is the model's stored memory of the conversation and grows with its length.

## The problem
The two parts want opposite things. Attention needs lots of memory per user, because every user's KV cache must sit on the GPU. The expert layer wants many users' words batched together, because GPUs are most efficient on big batches.

When both parts share the same GPU, long conversations eat the memory. Fewer users fit at once. The expert layer then gets small batches and wastes much of the GPU's power. The authors measured this directly: expert efficiency falls as context grows, while attention stays flat.

A known fix is attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD): put attention and experts on different GPUs. It helped on older hardware. The open question was whether it still pays on Nvidia's GB200 NVL72, a rack of 72 GPUs with very fast links, where the normal setup is already strong.

## The idea
Picture a restaurant. Waiters (attention GPUs) take orders and keep track of each table. Cooks (expert GPUs) prepare food. If every waiter also has to cook, each one can only serve a few tables, and the stove sits half-used. Split the jobs. Many waiters collect orders from many tables, then send them in bulk to a shared kitchen. Waiters serve more tables, and the cooks always have full pans.

The catch is that orders must travel between rooms on every layer of the model. FastAFD's job is to make that travel fast and hidden behind other work.

## How it works
1. **Split the roles.** Attention workers keep the KV cache, run attention, and decide which experts each word goes to. Expert workers hold the expert weights, which are over 90% of the model's parameters.
2. **Free up memory.** Because attention GPUs no longer store expert weights, they can hold 1.5 times as many users' conversations at once.
3. **Move words over the GPU links directly.** Words are sent to expert GPUs and results come back using GPU-side communication code (adapted from DeepEP), so the CPU does not slow things down.
4. **Fuse the expert work.** One long-running GPU program on the expert side processes every layer and every mini-batch from a task table, instead of launching many small jobs.
5. **Plan ahead.** A coordinator prepares the next step's plan while the GPUs are still running the current one, so no time is lost between steps.

## Results
Tests used two open MoE models, Qwen3-235B and MiniMax-M2.5, with 8,000- and 16,000-token conversations. The baseline was vLLM, a popular serving system, running the standard shared layout on the same hardware.

FastAFD produced 1.35 to 1.45 times more tokens per second per GPU. That counts the expert GPUs too. In practice, a cluster serving 100 users could serve about 140 with the same hardware.

The gain comes from capacity, not speed per reply. Each step takes about as long as before, but more users are served in each step. The team's simple formula predicted the measured speedups almost exactly (for example, 1.45 predicted and 1.45 measured).

The fused expert program cut step time by 42–44%. Turning off the plan-ahead coordinator cost 23% throughput and made FastAFD slower than the baseline.

## Why it matters
Serving costs dominate the price of AI products. A 40% gain in output per GPU, with no change to the model itself, is real money for anyone running large MoE models. The work also gives operators a clear rule for when splitting pays off, so they can plan hardware ratios instead of guessing. The code is open source.

## Caveats
It only covers the steady "writing" phase, not the initial reading of the prompt. It has not been combined with other common tricks like speculative decoding. The gains vanish once the expert side becomes the bottleneck, which happened inside the tested range for one model. Projections for future Nvidia hardware are estimates, not measurements. The baseline was compared on a single node.

## Key terms
- **Mixture-of-Experts (MoE):** a model made of many specialist sub-networks, where each word visits only a few.
- **Attention:** the step where the model looks back over earlier words.
- **KV cache:** the stored memory of a conversation, which grows with its length.
- **Disaggregation:** running different parts of a job on separate machines.
- **Throughput:** how much output a system produces per second.
- **NVL72:** an Nvidia rack that links 72 GPUs as if they were one big machine.

papers.title: Recursive Sparse Attention: Million-Token Length Extrapolation at Logarithmic Cost
papers.tldr: By organizing a model's memory into a tree of summaries and searching only promising branches, a 4B model trained on 32K-token texts reads up to 2 million tokens accurately and several times faster.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
Recursive Sparse Attention (RecSA) lets a language model trained on 32,000-token texts read documents of one to two million tokens, by searching its memory like a tree instead of rereading everything.

## Background you need
Language models read text as tokens, which are small chunks of words. In attention, the model's main reading step, each new token looks back at every earlier token to decide what matters. The model keeps a KV cache (its short-term memory of everything it has already read) so it does not recompute the past. A model's "context length" is how much text it can hold in view at once.

## The problem
Attention gets painfully slow on very long inputs. Every new token must scan the whole KV cache, so cost grows with the length of the text. At a million tokens, that is a lot of scanning for every single word the model writes.

There is a second problem. Training a model on million-token documents needs million-token documents, and those are rare. Most models are trained on much shorter texts. When you push them past that length, accuracy collapses.

Earlier shortcuts, called sparse attention, only look at a few chunks of the past. But most of them still score every chunk to decide which to look at. So the cost still grows with length, just more slowly.

## The idea
Think of a librarian looking for a fact in a huge archive. She does not open every box. She reads the label on each aisle, picks the promising aisles, then reads the shelf labels, then the box labels, and only then opens a few boxes. The work grows with the number of levels, not the number of boxes.

RecSA builds exactly this kind of label hierarchy over the model's memory. Each "label" is a short summary of a group of tokens. The model walks down the tree, opening only the most promising branches. Doubling the text adds roughly one more level, not double the work. Engineers call this logarithmic cost.

## How it works
1. **Build the tree.** Every 16 tokens in memory are grouped under one parent node. Each node stores a summary key (what the group is about) and an averaged value (what the group says). Groups of 16 nodes form the next level up, and so on.
2. **Search from the top.** For each new token, the model scores the candidates at the top level. It keeps up to 256 of them and moves down into their children. At the bottom, it reads the exact original tokens it selected.
3. **Don't throw away the rest.** The summaries of branches it skipped still get a small vote alongside the exact tokens. So far-away context is blurred, not erased.
4. **Keep distances familiar.** Models use positional encoding (a way to tell how far apart two tokens are). RecSA numbers each candidate by its place in the short candidate list, not its real position. So the model never sees a distance bigger than it saw in training.
5. **Train cheaply in two stages.** First, a tiny "pooler" that writes the summaries (about 25,000 numbers per layer) is trained to mimic what full attention would focus on. Then the main model is fine-tuned to work with the tree. Total training was 0.62 billion tokens, all at 32,000-token length.

## Results
The team started from Qwen3-4B, an open model with 4 billion parameters. They tested on RULER, a benchmark that hides facts in long texts and asks the model to find them.

At one million tokens, RecSA scored 60.5. The best competing method scored 40.0. At two million tokens, RecSA scored 49.3, versus 34.0 for the best rival. One common trick for extending context (YaRN) fell to near zero at these lengths.

On short everyday tasks, it stayed close to the original model. For example, it scored 70.5 on MMLU (a broad knowledge test) versus 70.1 before.

It is also faster. On one H200 GPU, reading a 524,000-token prompt took 80 seconds instead of 257, about 3 times faster. Writing each new token at that length took about 6 milliseconds instead of 23. At two million tokens, each new token took about 11 milliseconds, versus nearly 3 seconds for full attention.

## Why it matters
Million-token context means a model could hold an entire codebase, a long legal case, or months of chat history at once. RecSA suggests you can get there without training on million-token data and without huge compute bills. That makes long-context models cheaper to build and to run, including on a single GPU with memory moved to the computer's main RAM.

## Caveats
All main results use one 4-billion-parameter model, so it is unclear how it scales to bigger models. RULER is a synthetic test; real-world long-document evidence is thinner. Accuracy still drops as texts get longer. At short lengths (32,000 tokens), plain attention is still slightly faster. The method needs custom GPU code, which adds engineering effort.

## Key terms
- **Attention:** the step where each token decides which earlier tokens to focus on.
- **KV cache:** the model's stored memory of everything it has read so far.
- **Sparse attention:** looking at only a chosen subset of past tokens instead of all of them.
- **Logarithmic cost:** work that grows by a fixed step each time the input doubles.
- **Positional encoding:** how a model knows the order and distance between tokens.
- **Length extrapolation:** working well on inputs longer than any seen in training.

papers.title: KOSMOS: Self-scheduling Persistent Kernels for Communication-Compute Overlap
papers.tldr: GPU worker groups that grab whichever data-transfer or math task is ready next, instead of following a fixed plan, speed up large-model training on AMD MI350X/MI355X GPUs by 1.1x to 1.8x.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
KOSMOS is a set of GPU programs that let groups of GPU workers decide for themselves, moment to moment, whether to move data or do math, so big AI models train 10–83% faster on AMD's newest GPUs.

## Background you need
Large AI models are trained across many GPUs at once. To split one model across GPUs, engineers use tensor and sequence parallelism (cutting each layer's math and each text sequence into slices on different GPUs) and expert parallelism (placing different "expert" sub-networks of a Mixture-of-Experts model on different GPUs). Both require GPUs to constantly swap partial results. These swaps are called collectives. A kernel is a single program that runs on the GPU, and a GPU is split into many small processing units that run groups of threads called workgroups.

## The problem
While GPUs swap data, the math units often sit idle, and while they compute, the network links sit idle. The ideal is overlap: compute on data that has already arrived while the rest is still in transit.

Existing "fused" kernels try to do this, but with fixed plans. Some workgroups are permanently assigned to communication and others to computation. Or the work is split into chunks using a schedule tuned ahead of time. Real data does not arrive on a fixed timetable, so these plans leave gaps. Tuning the split for every model shape and cluster is also tedious.

When the swap sits on the critical path (the chain of steps that sets total training time), every idle microsecond adds up over millions of training steps.

## The idea
Picture a restaurant kitchen where staff are not given fixed jobs. Instead, there is a ticket rail ordered by what the dining room needs next. Any cook who is free grabs the most urgent ticket, whether it is "carry plates in from the delivery truck" or "cook this dish." Nobody waits for a manager to reassign them.

KOSMOS makes GPU workgroups behave like those cooks. They pull tasks from shared queues ordered by what downstream steps need first. A workgroup can move data one moment and do matrix math the next, depending on what is ready.

## How it works
1. **Persistent kernels.** Instead of launching many short programs, KOSMOS launches one long-lived program that stays on the GPU and keeps pulling work.
2. **Demand-ordered queues.** Tasks wait in queues sorted by when their results will be needed by the next step (the "consumer").
3. **Self-scheduling roles.** Each workgroup takes the next ready task and switches between communication and computation as data becomes available. There is no central scheduler, no cost model consulted on each call, and no hand-tuned split.
4. **Fusing collectives with matrix math.** For tensor and sequence parallelism, each data swap is merged into one kernel together with the matrix multiplication (GEMM) that uses it.
5. **Whole expert layers in one launch.** For Mixture-of-Experts models, sending tokens to experts, running the experts, and sending results back happens in one kernel launch per direction.

## Results
All tests ran on AMD Instinct MI350X and MI355X GPUs.

For tensor-plus-sequence-parallel training in Megatron-LM (a widely used training framework), KOSMOS was 1.10 to 1.28 times faster using BF16 numbers (a common 16-bit format). With MXFP8 (a newer, more compact 8-bit format), it was 1.10 to 1.25 times faster. In practice, a training run that took 10 days could finish in roughly 8 to 9.

For end-to-end training of proxy versions of DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen3-235B (two large Mixture-of-Experts models), KOSMOS was 1.29 to 1.83 times faster than DeepEP, a popular open-source library for expert communication. At the top end, that nearly halves the time spent per training step.

## Why it matters
Training frontier models costs enormous sums, and communication overhead is a large slice of it. A drop-in library that recovers 10–80% of that time, without per-model tuning, saves money and energy. It also strengthens the software ecosystem around AMD GPUs, which matters for anyone hoping for more competition in AI hardware.

## Caveats
The results here come from the paper's abstract; we could not access the full text for this summary, so details on test sizes are limited. All tests were on AMD hardware, so it is unclear how the approach performs on Nvidia GPUs. The Mixture-of-Experts results use "proxy" models (smaller stand-ins), not the full-size models. Persistent kernels are also harder to debug and maintain than ordinary ones.

## Key terms
- **Kernel:** a single program that runs on a GPU.
- **Workgroup:** a team of GPU threads that runs part of a kernel together.
- **Collective:** an operation where many GPUs exchange or combine data.
- **Overlap:** doing computation while communication is still in progress.
- **Persistent kernel:** a long-running GPU program that keeps pulling new tasks instead of exiting.
- **Mixture-of-Experts:** a model made of many specialist sub-networks, where each token visits only a few.

papers.title: HITCH: Teaching a Vision-Language Model to Operate a Humanoid through a Whole-Body Harness
papers.tldr: A simple control layer lets a vision-language model point at things and give body commands to a humanoid, reaching 95% success on a benchmark with just five examples per task and working on a real Unitree G1.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
HITCH gives an AI model that understands images and language a simple "control panel" for a humanoid robot, so the model can point at things and issue body commands while a separate learned controller handles balance and movement.

## Background you need
A vision-language model (VLM) is an AI that can look at images and read and write text, like the models behind modern chat assistants. A humanoid is a robot shaped like a person, with legs, a torso, arms and a head. Controlling a humanoid is hard because every motion must keep the robot balanced. A harness, in this paper's sense, is a software layer that turns high-level requests into low-level robot actions.

## The problem
VLMs are good at understanding scenes and planning steps ("pick up the box, walk to the table"). But they cannot directly drive dozens of motors while keeping a robot upright. They also do not naturally know where things are in 3D space, only where they appear in a picture.

So researchers need two things. First, a reliable interface that lets the model say what it wants the body to do. Second, reusable know-how about how to use that body for common tasks. Without these, each new task needs new robot training data, which is slow and expensive to collect, especially for humanoids.

## The idea
Think of a film director and a stunt performer. The director looks at the set and says "go to that door, pick up the suitcase, look left." The performer handles the footwork and balance. The director never has to think about knees and ankles.

In HITCH, the VLM is the director. The harness gives it two kinds of tools: a way to measure the scene, and a way to give body-level commands. A learned whole-body controller is the stunt performer.

## How it works
1. **Point to measure.** The VLM picks any point in a camera image, and the harness returns that point's 3D location. This turns "that box in the picture" into "a box 1.2 metres ahead and slightly left."
2. **Command body parts.** The VLM issues commands for the pelvis, torso, hands, walking and gaze direction, for example "move right hand here" or "walk to this spot."
3. **Track the motion.** A learned tracker converts these commands into coordinated motions of the whole body, keeping the robot balanced.
4. **Learn from teachers.** Teacher policies (pre-built solvers) complete five base tasks through the harness. Their step-by-step tool use is recorded as training examples.
5. **Fine-tune the VLM.** The VLM is trained on these recorded trajectories, so it learns general habits for using the body, not one specific task.

## Results
The authors first show that both halves matter. More accurate scene measurement and more accurate execution of commands each raised task success.

After fine-tuning on the five base tasks only, the VLM completed 51% of episodes on SIMPLE and 42.5% on HumanoidArena, two benchmarks of humanoid tasks it had not been specifically trained for. In practice, it succeeded about half the time on new jobs with zero task-specific examples.

Adding just five example trajectories per SIMPLE task raised SIMPLE success to 95%. That is a big jump from a tiny amount of extra data.

On a real Unitree G1 humanoid, the model carried a box and walked it to a goal, without any training data collected on the real robot.

## Why it matters
If general AI models can drive humanoids through a clean interface, new tasks could be taught with a handful of examples instead of thousands. That could make household and warehouse humanoids far cheaper to adapt. It also separates the "thinking" part from the "balancing" part, so each can improve on its own.

## Caveats
This summary is based on the paper's abstract and project details; we could not access the full text, so finer details are limited. The real-robot demonstration covers one task. Half the benchmark episodes still fail without task examples. Results depend on the quality of the learned tracker and the 3D measurement tool, which may struggle in cluttered or unfamiliar settings.

## Key terms
- **Vision-language model (VLM):** an AI that understands both images and text.
- **Humanoid:** a robot built in roughly human shape.
- **Harness:** a software layer that translates high-level requests into robot actions.
- **Whole-body controller (tracker):** a learned system that moves all joints together while keeping balance.
- **Teacher policy:** an existing solver whose actions are recorded as training examples.
- **Fine-tuning:** further training of an existing model on a smaller, focused dataset.

papers.title: Exploring Weight-Space Programming: Capabilities, Generalization, and Limitations
papers.tldr: An AI agent improved a small model by directly editing a few of its internal numbers, with no training, sometimes by 29 points on math, but the gains were uneven and often did not hold up.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
This paper tests whether an AI agent can improve another AI model by directly editing its internal numbers, with no training, and finds big but unreliable gains.

## Background you need
A language model is defined by billions of numbers called weights (or parameters). Normally, you improve a model by training it: showing it examples and letting an algorithm nudge all the weights a little. Weight-Space Programming (WSP) is a newer idea. A capable AI agent looks inside a smaller model, diagnoses why it fails, and rewrites specific weights by hand, like a programmer patching code.

## The problem
Training is expensive and opaque. It needs data, compute, and many passes, and it is hard to say why the new model is better. If an agent could find the exact few numbers that cause a failure and fix them, improvement could be cheaper and more understandable.

An earlier study showed an agent could fix a small model's math skills this way, mostly by stopping it from getting stuck in reasoning loops. But nobody knew how general this was. Does it work on other tasks? Do the fixes carry over? Does it work every time?

## The idea
Think of a mechanic who, instead of replacing the whole engine, listens to the car, finds the one loose bolt, and tightens it. The mechanic here is a strong AI model (GPT-6 Astra). The car is a small open model (Qwen3.5, in 0.8-billion and 9-billion-parameter sizes). The paper asks: how often does the mechanic find the right bolt?

## How it works
1. **Give the agent a workshop.** The agent works in a Python environment where it can inspect the small model's weights. A separate GPU runs the small model so the agent can test it.
2. **Let it probe.** The agent can ask the model to answer questions, or look at its internal activity (which parts "light up") on given inputs. It gets a budget of 50 test runs and up to 300 analysis scripts.
3. **Let it edit.** The agent can change weights inside the model's transformer layers (the repeated building blocks of the model). Allowed moves include small targeted changes to individual neurons and scaling attention heads up or down. It cannot use gradients, the standard training signal.
4. **Choose honestly.** The agent judges its edits only on practice questions. It may keep the original model if nothing clearly helps. Final scores come from separate, unseen test questions.
5. **Repeat across tasks.** The team ran 16 editing attempts over seven benchmarks, covering math, science, instruction-following, medicine, and coding.

## Results
On the small 0.8-billion model, the gains could be huge. Changing just 1,023 weights raised its score on MATH-500 (a set of competition-style math problems) from 8.35% to 37.80%. That is a jump of 29.45 points from editing a tiny fraction of the model. Its score on IFEval, a test of following formatting instructions, rose from 21.4% to 58.1%.

Some fixes spread to other skills. The math-edited model also improved on science questions (SciBench, +20.1 points) and instruction-following (+12.2 points) without further edits. But coding (SciCode) did not move at all.

On the larger 9-billion model, gains were small, around 2–3 points. One math edit looked great on practice questions (+29.7 points) but slightly hurt the real test score (−0.35). Six of the 16 attempts ended by keeping the original weights.

Reruns of the same math task gave +29.45, +5.00 and +27.30 points. All three edited the same layer, but changed very different numbers of weights.

## Why it matters
This is an early, honest map of a strange new ability: AI systems repairing other AI systems at the level of raw numbers. If it becomes reliable, it could make model fixes cheaper and easier to explain. It could also help researchers understand what specific weights do. The paper's careful negative results matter too, because they show where hype about this idea outruns the evidence.

## Caveats
Most tasks were tried only once, so the true spread of outcomes is unclear. Practice-set gains often did not hold on the real test. The small model had a lot of room to improve, which may inflate gains. The authors do not fully understand why successful edits work. Longer reasoning and agent tasks were not tested. A few numbers differ slightly between the paper's text and tables.

## Key terms
- **Weights (parameters):** the numbers inside a model that determine its behavior.
- **Training:** improving a model by repeatedly nudging its weights based on examples.
- **Gradient:** the standard signal that tells training which way to nudge each weight.
- **Weight-Space Programming:** an agent directly inspecting and rewriting a model's weights.
- **Held-out test:** questions kept hidden during editing, used for the final score.
- **Transfer:** when a fix for one skill also improves a different skill.
